summary: Module 1 pretest (AI-Augmented Engineering). Setup checks: Python 3.11.5, node v23.1.0, git 2.47.1 â€” all pass. Tooling: using opencode as the AI coding agent (agent mode â€” it reads files, runs commands, and makes changes autonomously); OS Windows with PowerShell. Self-rating: strong â€” I decompose work for AI, review output critically (I have spent the prior 17 modules reviewing and verifying AI/agent-produced changes against a live service), and iterate efficiently with probe scripts and regression tests. (2) The API that runs but ignores input validation and embeds the DB connection string in code: I would NOT accept it â€” I would review and require the AI to move credentials to environment config (settings layer, not source), and add input validation at the schema boundary; then write tests proving both behaviors (invalid payload rejected, config reads from env, no secrets in source). This is the review mindset: running code is the floor, not the bar. (3) When NOT to use AI to write code: when the code is security-critical and the cost of a subtly wrong but plausible output exceeds the speed gain, or when I do not understand the code well enough to review it â€” if I cannot audit the diff, I should not let an agent write it. (4) Reviewing AI code I don't understand: ask the AI to explain it, then decide â€” shipping code I cannot explain is how silent bugs reach production; rewriting it myself wastes the tool's value. (5) Reviewing 200 lines: read it as a diff with intent â€” check the boundary contracts (input validation, error paths, config), look for the classic failure classes (unbounded input, missing finally, shared mutable state, unchecked assumptions), and run targeted probes/tests rather than reading every line linearly. (6) Context: give the AI useful context upfront â€” a well-specified task with constraints (schema, contract, tests) produces correct output faster than many small ambiguous prompts, because each small prompt loses the thread; upfront context also lets me hold the agent accountable to the spec. (7) Three plausible solutions: pick by evidence â€” compare each against the stated constraints (correctness, maintainability, testability, performance) and the acceptance tests; if genuinely tied, pick the most testable/simplest and explain the choice in the PR. (8) Biggest risk of AI-generated code in production: plausible-but-wrong code that passes happy-path tests while failing on edge cases, security, or resource boundaries â€” because it looks correct, it skips the scrutiny that catches human mistakes.
